name: Snare
description: a loop of vine on a bent stick. catches small game.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a snare. A loop, a stick, an animal.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: vine (muscadine or bush) + stick (tree branch). The loop goes on a game trail.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Bend the stick, tie the vine, set the loop where they run. Opossums wander into them after dark — the easiest meat you'll ever trap.

name: Deadfall Trap
description: a heavy stone propped on sticks. crushes whatever trips it — set big on a deer trail and it can take a deer.

knowledgeLevels.1: A deadfall. Stone, sticks, bait. Simple and brutal.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 sticks + 1 heavy stone + bait (berries or nuts). The trigger is the trick.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can build one. Balance the stone, set the trigger, bait it. Check daily. Set it big on a deer trail and once in a long while it takes a deer — mostly you'll dress rabbit.

name: Box Trap
description: a woven sapling cage with a drop door. for medium game — raccoon, opossum, muskrat, the occasional fox... and sometimes a skunk, which you will regret.

knowledgeLevels.1: A box trap. Woven saplings, a drop door, bait inside. For clever medium game.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 4 sticks + 2 vine + bait (meat scraps work best). The door counterweights shut behind them.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can build one. Set it by dens and water for raccoon and muskrat, on night trails for opossum. Foxes are shy of traps — bait it well, leave it alone, check at dawn. Groundhogs funnel straight into one set at a burrow mouth; beavers take a big one set on a slide; bobcats are fox-shy but the same bait works. Armadillos blunder in wherever they root — they barely look where they're going. Skunks wander in too: open it from upwind, with a long stick, and have a change of clothes. A rattlesnake in the box means the weave held and your luck did too — pin it before you reach in.

name: Fish Weir
description: stakes and vine woven across shallow water. crayfish funnel in; turtles too.

knowledgeLevels.1: A fish weir. Stakes and vine in the shallows — funnels them in, keeps them in.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 3 sticks + 2 vine. Drive the stakes in a V, leave a gap with the basket at the throat.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can weave one. Set it in creek or wetland shallows. Crayfish pile in; a turtle is a bonus — mind your fingers, they bite.

name: Woven cloth
description: plant fiber twisted and woven tight. not pretty, but it holds water back.

knowledgeLevels.1: Woven plant fiber. Someone made cloth from weeds.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 3 plant fiber. Twist the fibers into cord, weave the cords tight.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can weave it. Twist fiber into two-ply cord, then plain-weave over-under. Tight enough to strain water.

name: Water Filter
description: cloth and charcoal layered in any container. makes murky water safe.

knowledgeLevels.1: A filter. Dirty water in, clean out.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: cloth + charcoal (from fire). Layer them in a container.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Cloth on bottom, charcoal, pour through.

name: Cooking Spit
description: a stick over fire. cooks meat evenly.

knowledgeLevels.1: Meat on a stick over fire. Better than raw.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 1 sturdy stick. Green wood (will not burn).
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Cook meat = +50% calories, safe to eat.

name: Stone knife
description: flint knapped to an edge, bound with vine. cuts meat, wood, cord.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a sharp edge. Stone breaks sharp.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: stone + vine. Strike the stone to knap an edge, bind it with vine.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can knap one. A few good strikes, a working edge. The oldest tool there is.

name: Spring-Pole Snare
description: a bent sapling staked down, a vine loop on a game trail. the sapling does the lifting — the loop only has to be in the right place.

knowledgeLevels.1: A snare with a bent sapling for a spring. Faster than a plain loop.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 vine + 2 sticks + bait. The sapling does the lifting — the loop only has to be in the right place.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can build one. Bend the sapling down, stake it, run the vine loop on a game trail and tie off to the trigger. Foxes take these on night trails; turkeys walk into them on dusting flats. A loop set low on a goose trail will take a goose now and then — they step right through. Crows are too wary for most sets, but one strutting a bait line will commit. Check at dawn — a spring-pole holds its catch off the ground, away from other teeth.

name: Funnel Fish Basket
description: branches woven into a funnel, wide at the mouth and narrow at the throat. fish swim in; the weave keeps them.

knowledgeLevels.1: A woven funnel basket. Fish swim in, the weave keeps them.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 4 branches + 2 vine. Weave the funnel narrow at the throat, wide at the mouth; stake it facing downstream.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can weave one. Set it in the creek throat where the water narrows, mouth upstream. Chub and crayfish pile in overnight. A snapping turtle is a bonus and a hazard — pin the head before you reach past it.

name: Turkey Noose Pole
description: sticks lashed into a long pole with a vine slip-noose at the end. for birds that roost in low branches.

knowledgeLevels.1: A long pole with a slip noose at the end. For birds that sleep in low branches.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 3 sticks (lashed long) + 1 vine + bait. The noose cinches when you pull.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Lash the sticks into a pole, tie the vine noose, bait the clearing and wait for dusk. Turkeys roost low; slip the noose over the head and pull sharp. Miss and the whole flock is gone for a week.

name: Trotline
description: a vine line strung bank to bank with baited drops hanging off it. fishes while you sleep.

knowledgeLevels.1: A line strung across the creek with baited drops. Fishes while you sleep.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 1 stick + 3 vine + bait (2). Tie drop lines along the main line, bait each, anchor both banks.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can rig one. Stretch the vine across a narrow run, hang the drops a hand deep, bait with whatever is going soft. Run it at dawn and dusk. A turtle on the line means the line held and your luck did — cut it loose from upstream.

name: Drying Rack
description: a raised frame of lashed sticks. air and thin smoke do the preserving; the rack just holds the meat up where the dogs cannot reach.

knowledgeLevels.1: A rack for drying meat and fish. Air does the work.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 wood + 4 sticks. Lash a frame waist-high, keep it over thin smoke.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can lash one. Hang thin strips over faint smoke, not flame. Two dry days and the meat keeps. This is how winter gets survived.

name: Stone Axe
description: a knapped stone head bound to a wood handle with vine. fells saplings, splits kindling, and drives the stakes your traps stand on.

knowledgeLevels.1: A stone head on a wood handle. The oldest axe there is.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: stone + wood + 2 vine. Knap the edge, seat the head, bind it tight and let the vine dry to shrink.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. It will not fell an oak, but it will take saplings and split kindling all day. Rebind it when the vine loosens.

name: Braided Cord
description: plant fiber twisted and braided into cord. binds everything a vine can bind, and fits in a pocket.

knowledgeLevels.1: Twisted plant fiber, strong as thin rope.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 4 fiber. Twist two strands against each other, feed in more as you go, braid three twisted strands.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can twist it. Roll fiber on your thigh until it kinks, let it ply back on itself, braid three plies. Slow work, strong cord.

name: Minnow Trap
description: a small woven funnel, baited. minnows and crayfish swim in looking for the meal; the weave keeps them. the surest way to turn scraps into bait for bigger fishing.

knowledgeLevels.1: A little funnel basket with bait inside. Small fish go in, small fish stay in.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 3 branches + 2 vine + bait. Weave it tight — minnows slip anything loose. Set it in the shallows.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can weave one. Chub are the prize: not much meat on them, but a live chub on a line is how the real fish get caught.

name: Rabbit Stick
description: a short heavy throwing stick, weighted at one end. the oldest ranged weapon there is — for rabbits, squirrels, and birds too slow to matter.

knowledgeLevels.1: A throwing stick. Heavy end forward. Older than the bow and half as proud.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 1 wood log, shaped. Throw sidearm, lead the target — it flies flat and true to about twenty paces.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can shape one. Rabbits freeze before they run; that frozen second is the whole weapon. A squirrel on a trunk is a gift — throw for the far side so the stick clips it either way.

name: Pit Trap
description: a pit with sharpened stakes at the bottom, brushed over with leaves. labor to dig, brutal to fall in — deer and boar both. mark it well: your own pit will take you too.

knowledgeLevels.1: A pit with stakes in the bottom. Dig it on a trail, brush it over, wait.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 sticks (sharpened for the stakes). Dig it deep — chest deep for deer. Angle the stakes inward.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can dig one. It is a day's work with a digging stick and it ruins your hands, but a pit on a deer trail works while you sleep. Check it every morning. A boar in a pit is a butchering problem with teeth — spear it from above before you climb down.

name: Frog Gig
description: a stick with stone barbs lashed at the head. for frogs at night and fish in the shallows — pin, don't stab, and the barbs do the holding.

knowledgeLevels.1: A pronged spear for frogs. Night work, by light.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 1 stick + 1 stone (knapped to barbs) + fiber to lash. Pin the frog to the mud — a stab tears free.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can lash one. Walk the shallows slow with a light; frogs freeze in it. Pin, scoop, and the legs are yours. The same gig takes suckers and chub in daylight shallows.

name: Lean-To
description: two forked posts, a ridgepole, and a roof of branches shingled against the rain. the difference between sleeping through a storm and surviving one.

knowledgeLevels.1: A slanted roof on two posts. The first architecture.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 6 sticks + 4 branches + 2 fiber. Back to the wind, low end into the weather, roof shingled thick — water runs down, not through.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can raise one. Face the opening away from the prevailing wind, bed it with dry leaves, and keep the fire just outside the drip line. A good lean-to and a fire is the difference between a wet night and a dangerous one.

name: Fire Plow
description: a hardwood base and a rubbing stick. friction and patience — the plow groove fills with hot dust, and the dust becomes a coal. fire without a match, the hard way.

knowledgeLevels.1: Rubbing two sticks together. It is exactly as hard as the jokes say.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 wood logs — one soft for the base, one hard for the plow. Cut a groove, plow hard and fast, and have the tinder bundle ready BEFORE the coal comes.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can do it. Dry wood only, full-body pressure, and the coal dies in seconds if the tinder is not waiting. Blind attempts almost never work; your hands learn this in the failing. Once the coal is in the bundle, blow gentle — impatience kills more fires than rain.

name: Stone Boiler
description: fire-heated stones dropped in water. the stones do the boiling — soup, stew, and water made safe, no pot required.

knowledgeLevels.1: Hot rocks in water. The water boils; the rocks do not care.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 3 stones. Heat them till they glow dull red — never use stones from the creek, wet stones explode in fire.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can boil without a pot. Drop the stones in with sticks, fish them out the same way, repeat till it rolls. A watertight bark trough or a hide sling holds the water. This is how you make questionable water safe and thin soup into stew.

name: Squirrel Pole
description: a fallen log with snare loops set along it, each loop tied off to a sapling. squirrels run logs like highways — the pole just collects the toll.

knowledgeLevels.1: Snares set along a fallen log. Squirrels run the log; the loop does the rest.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 1 stick + 2 vine. Set the loops upright on the log where it crosses a trail, tied to a bent sapling that lifts the catch clear.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can set one. Find a log squirrels already run — bark worn smooth, droppings on top. Raccoons use the same highways at night, which is a bonus until it is a fight. Check at dawn and reset by noon.

name: Sharpened stick
description: a stick whittled to a point. Better than bare hands — barely, but barely counts.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen the shape: a stick, one end shaved to a point.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: stick. Shave one end to a point with a knife or a sharp stone edge. The point wants to be centered, not hooked.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can whittle one in minutes. The oldest spear there is — and still better than fists.

name: Hunting spear
description: long, balanced, stone-tipped. Reach is the difference between hunting and being hunted.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a hunting spear. Longer than a man, stone at the killing end.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: branch + stone + vine. Knap the stone to a point, notch the branch end, lash the head tight with vine. The lashing is the weapon — a loose head is a stick.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Straight branch, seasoned if you can wait. The head seats deep and the vine wraps wet so it shrinks tight. Thrust, don't throw — the throw is a different weapon.

name: Fire-hardened spear
description: a branch with the tip blackened and hard as iron. Fire did half the work.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a fire-hardened spear. The tip is black, polished, hard.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: branch + wood (for the fire). Shave the tip, then bake it in coals — not flame — turning slow. The heat drives the sap out and the wood goes iron-hard.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Coals, not flame: flame chars it weak, coals temper it. Scrape, heat, scrape, heat, until the point rings when you tap it.

name: Crude bow
description: bent stick, twisted cord. The arrows are straighter than the bow, which is fine.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a crude bow. A bent branch and a cord — simple enough to copy, hard enough to shoot.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: branch + vine. A green branch that bends without snapping, a cord twisted from vine fiber. The string wants to be shorter than the bow by a hand's width.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Tillering is the art: shave the belly until both limbs bend even. An uneven bow throws sideways and teaches you humility.

name: Bow
description: seasoned wood and twisted sinew. The arrow knows where it is going.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a real bow. Not a bent stick — a weapon, shaped with patience.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: wood + 2 vine. A seasoned stave, a cord braided tight from vine fiber, and days of shaving. The grip stays thick; the limbs taper.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. Season the wood or it follows the string and dies. Brace it low at first and watch the limbs — they tell you where they want wood removed.

name: Crossbow
description: crank, lock, loose. Less art than the bow, more certainty.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a crossbow. A bow on a stock, held at full draw by a catch.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 wood + vine + fiber. A stout stock, a short strong bow, a cord, and a trigger notch. The catch is the whole weapon — everything else is carpentry.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. The stock carries the draw so your arms don't have to. Cut the nut from hardwood and test the catch a hundred times before you trust it near your face.

name: Sling
description: two cords and a pouch. David's technology, still working.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen a sling. Two cords, a pouch, a stone — and range that embarrasses bows.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 fiber. Braid two cords, weave a pouch between them. One cord has a loop for the finger; the other just a knot to let go.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make one. The release is everything: one smooth circle overhead, let the knot cord slip at the top. Stones are everywhere; accuracy is not, at first.

name: Arrow
description: straight, fletched, meant for something living. Made five at a time — arrows are ammunition, not heirlooms.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen arrows. Straight shafts, stone points, feathered tails.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 stick + stone + fiber. Straighten shafts over heat, knap small points, bind them on, fletch with whatever feathers or fiber you have. Five at a time — one arrow is a wish.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make them. Spine matters: too stiff and they fishtail, too soft and they wobble. Match the shaft to the bow and they fly like they mean it.

name: Crossbow bolt
description: short, thick, brutal. Built for penetration, not grace. Made five at a time.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen crossbow bolts. Short, heavy, all business.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 stick + stone. Short stout shafts, heavy knapped heads. No fletching needed at this range — mass does the work.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make them. Keep them short and heavy; the crossbow's power forgives ugly. Five at a time, always — a crossbow with one bolt is a club.

name: Bark armor
description: bark lashed with vine. Better than skin.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen bark armor. Plates of bark laced together, worn like a shell.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 3 bark + 2 vine. Wide bark strips, dried flat under weight, laced overlapping like shingles with vine. Overlap downward — blows slide off.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make it. Soak the bark to shape it, dry it flat, lace it snug but not tight — it should move when you move. Won't stop a spear. Will stop the second claw.

name: Padded cloth wraps
description: layers of cloth tied tight. Better than skin. Barely.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen padded wraps. Cloth layered thick around arms and torso.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 cloth. Fold and quilt the cloth into thick pads, tie them where bites land — forearms, shoulders, thighs. Layers spread the force.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make them. Quilt, don't just stack: stitch or tie the layers so they can't slide apart on impact. Light, quiet, and better than nothing by a real margin.

name: Hide armor
description: cured hide, laced with sinew. Smells like work.

knowledgeLevels.1: You have seen hide armor. Tough cured skin, cut and laced into a cuirass.
knowledgeLevels.2: Materials: 2 hide + vine. Cure the hides (scrape, dry, work them soft), cut panels, lace with vine or sinew. The curing is the armor — raw hide rots, cured hide stops teeth.
knowledgeLevels.3: You can make it. Work the hide until it's supple or it cracks at the first bend. Double the chest, single the limbs. Heavy, hot, and worth every ounce when something big decides you're food.
